1. Introduction
The Three-Rivers headwater region (TRHR), located in the eastern Tibetan Plateau, is a complex collage
composed of multiple accreted terranes (e.g., Songpan-Ganzi, Eastern Qiangtang, Western Qiangtang,
Yidun, and South China) bounded by several sutures, which mark the closure of the eastern Paleo-Te-
thys Ocean (Figure 1). Many studies have suggested that the drift histories and amalgamation process-
es of these terranes involved continental-continental collisions (e.g., Chang et al., 1986; Ding et al., 2013;
Ma et al., 2019; Metcalfe, 2013; M. D. Yan et al., 2016; X. F. Yang et al., 2017; Y. G. Yan et al., 2019; Yin
& Harrison, 2000), accompanied by the evolution of the eastern segment of the Tethys Oceans (e.g., Cao
et al., 2019; Dan et al., 2018; Sengör, 1987; M. D. Yan et al., 2016). Thus, recognizing the paleopositions of
the above-mentioned terranes and the closure times of the Tethys Oceans are crucial to understand the
pre-Cenozoic evolution of the Tibetan Plateau. Over the past decades, although it has generally been accept-
ed that the TRHR was characterized by an archipelago of arcs or continental ribbons separating multiple
seaways within the late Paleozoic-early Mesozoic Paleo-Tethys, the evolution process and closure time of
© 2021. American Geophysical Union.
All Rights Reserved. the eastern part of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean have remained uncertain (e.g., Reid et al., 2005; Zi et al., 2012).

sampling positions in the Gadikao Fm.
For example, the estimated closure time of the huge Paleo-Jinsha Ocean ranges from the Late Permian (Sha
& Fürsich, 1999) to the Early-Middle Triassic (Pullen et al., 2008; Zi et al., 2012), the Late Triassic (Dan
et al., 2018; C. Li et al., 2009; P. P. Song et al., 2015), the Early Jurassic (Ding et al., 2013), the Middle Jurassic
(Xiao et al., 2005) or even to the mid-Cretaceous (Yin & Harrison, 2000), based on different approaches from
paleontologic, paleomagnetic, magmatic, and sedimentologic analyses.
The Eastern Qiangtang Terrane (EQT) is juxtaposed with the Songpan-Ganzi Terrane, the Western Qiang-
tang Terrane (WQT), the South China Block (SCB) and the Yidun Terrane along the three major Paleo-Teth-
yan suture zones, namely, the Jinsha, Longmucuo-Shuanghu and Ganzi-Litang suture zones (Figure 1).

### page_3
Geophysical Research Letters 10.1029/2020GL092059
The EQT is one of the key terranes involved in the tectonic evolution of the Paleo-Tethys (e.g., Gehrels
et al., 2011; Metcalfe, 2013; Yin & Harrison, 2000). Determining its drift history is crucial to solve the tec-
tonic evolution of the east Paleo-Tethys.
Paleomagnetism is a powerful method for quantitative paleogeographic reconstruction. Some paleomagnet-
ic studies have been carried out to constrain the late Paleozoic-early Mesozoic formation of the Qiangtang
Terrane, such as in the Tuotuohe (Cheng et al., 2013; Song et al., 2015, 2017; X. F. Yang et al., 2017) and
Yanshiping areas (M. D. Yan et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2019; P. P. Song et al., 2020) in the central EQT and the
Raggyorcaka-Woruoshan area in the west EQT (Cheng et al., 2012; C. Y. Song et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2019)
and WQT (C. Y. Song et al., 2012) (Figure 1a). These results provide a basic framework for the paleolatitude
evolution of the Permian-Triassic in this region. To date, however, few late Paleozoic-early Mesozoic paleo-
magnetic results have been obtained from the eastern EQT, which is a vital linkage region in the TRHR. At
present, there is only one Late Permian result (age still controversial) from sedimentary rocks near Markam
(K. N. Huang et al., 1992) and two low-quality Permian-Triassic results from Derchin (X. Z. Li et al., 1999;
Figure 1). Given the narrow and long ( 1,500 km) shape of the EQT, the lack of robust paleomagnetic data
from the region have severely hindered∼ our understanding on the paleogeography and the evolution of the
Eastern Paleo-Tethys in the TRHR.
In this study, we report results of a new paleomagnetic and U-Pb geochronologic study of the poorly age
constrained (previously assigned to be the late Paleozoic) Gadikao Fm. from the eastern EQT, which is now
dated to have formed close to the P/T boundary. Integrating our new data with previously available suitable
quality paleomagnetic results and other lines of geologic evidence, we refine the Permo-Triassic drift history
of the EQT and estimate the closure time of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean in the TRHR.
2. Geologic Setting and Paleomagnetic Sampling
The EQT, also known as the “Northern Qiangtang” Terrane, is located within the central Tibetan Plateau
(Figure 1a). Geologically, it is separated from the Songpan-Ganze terrane by the Jinsha suture zone to the
north and from the WQT by the Longmu Co-Shuanghu suture zone-Taniantaweng orogenic arc to the south
(K. N. Huang et al., 1992; C. Li et al., 2009; M. D. Yan et al., 2016; T. N. Yang et al., 2011). Based on the
stratigraphic characteristics, to date, there are no direct records indicating the existence of a metamorphic
crystalline basement in the EQT (Pullen et al., 2008). The oldest sedimentary rocks are Early Ordovician
in age, covered by Late Devonian to Triassic to Cenozoic sedimentary sequences (Z. Z. Zhao et al., 2001).
The sedimentary sequences in the Zaduo area are the Lower Carboniferous Zaduo Group (Gr.), the Upper
Carboniferous Jiamainong Gr., the Permian Kaixinling Gr. and Gadikao Fm., the Middle Triassic Jielong
Fm., the Upper Triassic Jieza Gr., and the Middle Jurassic Quemocuo Fm. Two angular unconformities are
present between the Middle Triassic Jielong Fm. and the Upper Triassic Jieza Gr. and between the Upper
Triassic Jieza Gr. and the Middle Jurassic Quemocuo Fm. (QGS, 2005; Figure 1b and 1c). The rock types of
the Gadikao Fm. vary spatially, especially with regard to the abundance of volcanic rocks, forming a vol-
canic belt along the southern half of the EQT, from Zaduo in the west to Nangqian in the east (QGS, 2005).
The Gadikao Fm. is widely exposed in the Zaduo area. It consists mainly layers of rhyolitic tuff, rhyolite
dacite, crystalline glassy tuff, and volcanic breccia that are intercalated with limestone and siltstone, with
clear paleo-horizontal indicators in the field (Figure S1). Numerous fossils (fusulinids and brachiopods)
are present in the limestone beds (QGS, 2005; S. P. Li et al., 2008). The identified fossil brachiopods (e.g.,
Gigantoproductus cf. giganteus [Sowerby] and Delepinea depressa Ching et Liao) and corals (Kueichouphyl-
lum sp.) in the underlying sedimentary unit suggested an Early Carboniferous age (BGE & DQP, 1988),
and therefore the Gadikao Fm. was assigned to be an Early Carboniferous rock unit in the 1:200,000 Jiduo
regional geologic survey map. Later this formation provided a preliminary U-Pb zircon date of 287 ± 4 Ma
(S. P. Li et al., 2008). Because no sampling location, measuring procedure and data details were provided in
S. P. Li et al. (2008), the reliability of this data is still questionable. In addition, T. N. Yang et al. (2011) sug-
gested that the volcanic rock dominated Nuoribagaribao and Gadikao Fms. might have formed during the
Late Permian. Therefore, major uncertainties still exist for the age of the volcanic rocks in the Zaduo area.
The Sulu (SL) section (32°30.0′N and 95°10.0′E) is exposed as part of an anticline with a SE-NW-trending
fold axis (Figure 1b), which was formed during Middle to Late Triassic deformation (QGS, 2005). The folded

### page_4
Geophysical Research Letters 10.1029/2020GL092059
volcanic sequence of the Gadikao Fm., is exposed in two limbs, with clear bedding orientations (Figure 1b
and Figure S1). It is in fault contact with the underlying Lower Carboniferous Zaduo Gr. and unconform-
ably overlain by the Middle Jurassic Quemocuo Fm. (Figure 1b). The Gadikao Fm. has a thickness of over
200 m in the SL section. The upper part mainly consists of 15–20-m-thick at least six rhyolite dacite flows,
intercalated with thin-bedded sandstone, which provide b∼oth excellent structural control on the original
attitude of the lavas and evidence for episodic eruptions over a protracted period of time (Figure S1). Three
sites (SL1-3) were collected from the rhyolite dacite flows. Each site contains at least one discrete flow.
Underneath the rhyolite dacite flows is a 5-m-thick volcanic breccia layer, followed by cycles of crystal-
line glassy tuff and tuff layers ( 2–5 m ea∼ch), where an anticline is present at the bottom of the section.
Another 28 sites have been colle∼cted along the tuff layers (tuffaceous material fall deposits). A total of 318
core samples from 31 sites were collected from the SL section. In addition, three samples were taken from
the stratigraphic top, bottom and middle parts of the Gadikao Fm. for U-Pb zircon age determination. The
three samples are the rhyolite dacite (SL A) and the crystalline glassy tuff (SL B) at the northeast flank, and
the tuff (SL C) at the southwest side of the anticline, respectively. (Figure S1).
3. Zircon U-Pb Geochronology
Detailed analytical procedure and the cathode luminescence (CL) images for selected samples are described
in Text S2 in the supporting information. The cathodoluminescence images show that all the zircon grains
from samples SL A, B and C are generally transparent, euhedral to subhedral, have a prismatic shape with
clear oscillatory zoning (Figure S2). The lengths of the long axes of zircon grains are 80–150 μm and the
Th/U ratios are larger than 0.3, indicative of a magmatic origin (Table S1 in the supporting information).
The analyses of 23 zircon grains from the rhyolite dacite sample (SL A) yield a weighted mean 206Pb/238U
age of 248.1 ± 1.8 Ma (2σ; MSWD = 1.8; Figure S2d); 24 spot analyses of zircons from the crystalline glassy
tuff sample (SL B) yield a weighted mean 206Pb/238U age of 254.0 ± 1.2 Ma (2σ; MSWD = 0.86; Figure S2e),
whereas 23 zircon spots from the tuff sample (SL C), which is stratigraphically between samples SL A and
B, yield a weighted mean 206Pb/238U age of 252.8 ± 1.7 Ma (2σ; MSWD = 1.6; Figure S2f). Therefore, our de-
tailed U-Pb zircon analyses of the three volcanic samples from the stratigraphic top, middle and bottom part
of the Gadikao Fm. (Figures 1c and Figure S1) indicate that they are of volcanic origin and have age esti-
mates of 248.1 ± 1.8 Ma, 252.8 ± 1.7 Ma and 254.0 ± 1.2 Ma, respectively (Figure 1c, Figure S1 and S2). The
ages are reliable and consistent with the stratigraphic sequence and show that the age of the Gadikao Fm.
was around the P/T boundary. Similar U-Pb zircon data of the Nuoribagaribao Fm. in the Dongmozhazhua
area 40 km east of the Zaduo County were also reported (T. N. Yang et al., 2011), suggesting synchronous
volca∼nic eruptions across a large area of the region.
4. Paleomagnetic Results
Rock magnetic experiments and analysis, and paleomagnetic treatment, including thermal and alternating
field demagnetization analysis are described in Texts S3 and S4 in the supporting information. A total of
257 out of 318 specimens yield reliable ChRM directions that provide 29 out of 31 estimated site-mean
directions (Table S2). A total of 29 independent sites, 257 specimens (Figure 2, Table S2), with means of
22 normal and 7 reverse polarity. They provide an overall mean direction of D = 8.7°, I = 36.1°, k = 16.5,
g g g
α = 6.8° in situ, and D = 22.0°, I = 19.4°, k = 38.7, and α = 4.4° after tilt correction. The tilt-corrected α
95 s s s 95 95
(k) is smaller (larger) than that of in situ (from 6.8° [16.5] to 4.4° [38.7]), indicating an improved clustering
of site mean directions after tilt correction. The 29 site means yield positive McFadden (1990) and Watson
and Enkin (1993) fold and McFadden & McElhinny (1990) reversals tests (see details in Text S5), as well as
pass the paleosecular variation check (Text S5), likely yielding a primary paleopole of 59.7°N and 228.2°E
(A = 3.3°), with a paleolatitude of 10.0° ± 3.3°N for the study area.

5. Discussion
5.1. The Northward Drift of the EQT in the Permo-Triassic
In this study, we interpret the obtained ChRM directions to represent a Late Permian to Early Triassic geo-
magnetic field, and the new paleomagnetic pole (59.7°N, 228.2°E, A = 3.3°) is based on a reasonably large

data set and a high quality (29 sites, 257 samples, fulfill all the Van der Voo's, 1990 seven quality criteria)
for the EQT, with a corresponding paleolatitude of 10.0° ± 3.3°N during the 254–248 Ma time interval

To better understand the drift history of the EQT during the Permian to Triassic, all 17 available paleomag-
netic results from rocks in the region have been compiled (Table S3; Cheng et al., 2012, 2013, K. N. Huang
et al., 1992; Ma et al., 2019; X. Z. Li et al., 1999; Song et al., 2012; Song et al., 2015, 2017, 2020; X. F. Yang
et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2019). Given that ssthe EQT is long (over 1,500 km) and narrow, all the paleo-
magnetic directions were converted to the present study site (32.5°∼N and 95.2°E), the new paleolatitudes
were then recalculated and are shown in Figure 3 and Table S3. Because of differences in data quality, we
re-evaluate the above paleomagnetic data following the restrictive criteria for high-quality paleomagnetic
data that must satisfy the first five criteria of Van der Voo's (1990) (Besse & Courtillot, 2002): (1) well-de-
termined rock age (uncertainties<15 Myr or by accurate isotopic dating); (2) sufficient number of samples
(n ≥ 36 [specimens] and N ≥ 6 [sites]; k [or K] ≥ 10 and α [A ] ≤ 15°); (3) stepwise demagnetization; (4)
95 95
robust field tests (fold test or reversals test); and (5) structural control and craton coherence.
Among these 17 paleomagnetic data, 10 data sets cannot fulfill the above five criteria and were excluded
from our further analyses. For example, paleolatitude estimates of the Late Carboniferous-Early Permian
(23.5 ± 2.2°S, X. F. Yang et al., 2017), the Early-Middle Permian (11.2 ± 12.5°S, Cheng et al., 2012), the Late
Triassic (30.4 ± 4.0°N, C. Y. Song et al., 2012; 31.8 ± 5.6°N, Zhou et al., 2019) fail Criterion 1 due to their
large age uncertainties ( 25, 20 and 18 Myr, respectively); Paleolatitude of the Early Permian at 5.1 ± 7.2°S
by X. Z. Li et al. (1999) fa∼ils Criteria 2–5; Paleolatitudes of the Early-Middle Permian (11.2 ± 12.5°S, Cheng
et al., 2012), Middle Permian (16.5 ± 14.6°S, Cheng et al., 2013) and the Late Permian (12.9 ± 9.3°S, Cheng
et al., 2012; 5.5 ± 9.3°S, Cheng et al., 2013) fail Criterion two because of the small number of sampling sites
(both only have five sites); The Early Triassic paleolatitude of 4.8±6.7°N by Cheng et al. (2012) fails Criteri-
on 2, 4; and the Late Triassic latitude of 31.3 ± 8.8°N by X. Z. Li et al. (1999) fails all Criteria 1–5 (see details
of the data evaluation in the Text S6 and Table S3).
The remaining seven paleopoles seem to be high quality results that fulfill all the five criteria and with qual-
ity factor (Van der Voo, 1990) Q ≥ 6 (K. N. Huang et al., 1992; Ma et al., 2019; P. P. Song et al., 2015, 2017,
2020; Zhou et al., 2019; this study) (Table S3). However, after detailed analyses of the original data, the Late

Figure 3. Paleolatitude evolution of the Eastern Qiangtang Terrane (EQT), Tarim, Eurasia and Gondwana during
the Late Paleozoic to the Early Mesozoic. Paleolatitudes of Siberia-Eurasia and India-Gondwana are from Torsvik
et al. (2012), those of Tarim are from B. C. Huang et al. (2018). The paleomagnetic data of the EQT can be seen in
Table S3 (1, P. P. Song et al., 2017; 2, Ma et al., 2019; 3, This study; 4, P. P. Song et al., 2020; 5, P. P. Song et al., 2015),
where Tarim, Eurasia and Gondwana are in Table S4. The solid gray pentagon represents the paleomagnetic data from
Zhou et al. (2019). The orange filled circles represent the paleomagnetic data less qualified but seems still reliable from
C. Y. Song et al. (2012), X. F. Yang et al. (2017), and Zhou et al. (2019).
Permian paleomagnetic result of K. N. Huang et al. (1992) and the Early Triassic result of Zhou et al. (2019)
were excluded from our further analyses. For the Late Permian paleolatitude (4.6 ± 6.1°N, Q = 6) of K. N.
Huang et al. (1992), they assigned the studied sandstone Tuoba Fm. to the Longtanian (Wuchiapingian,
254–259 Ma), based on the fusulinid Codonofusiella in the section, which was later indicated to be older
∼than 268 Ma, based on a recent Rb-Sr data of 268.4 Ma for the overlying volcanic rock dominated Xiayacun
Fm. (TARGS, 2007) (see details in the Text S∼6). Thus, the age of the paleomagnetic results is controversial
and fail Criterion 1. Moreover, even if the assigned Longtanian age were correct, the obtained paleolatitude
of 4.6 ± 6.1°N of K. N. Huang et al. (1992) differs from a more robust contemporaneous result from volcanic
rocks of 5.0 ± 5.6°S at 259 Ma (Ma et al., 2019). For the Early Triassic paleomagnetic direction of Zhou
et al. (2019), there is an∼ obvious mistake in calculating the mean directions, resulting in a suspicious pale-
omagnetic pole (invalid even after recalculation), and hence the two results are excluded from our further
analysis (see details in the Text S6). Finally, there are only five high quality poles for the Permian-Triassic
EQT (Ma et al., 2019; P. P. Song et al., 2015, 2017, 2020; This study), four of which are from the central EQT
(e.g., Tuotuohe [P. P. Song et al., 2015, 2017] and Yanshiping [Ma et al., 2019; P. P. Song et al., 2020]), and this
study is from the eastern part of the EQT. These high-quality paleomagnetic latitude estimates indicate that
the EQT was located at 22.4 ± 4.7°S at 297 Ma (P. P. Song et al., 2017) and drifted northward to 5.0 ± 5.6°S
at 259 Ma (Ma et al., 2019), moving∼ to 10.0 ± 3.3°N at 251 Ma (this study), arriving 23.5 ± 5.6°N at
2∼40 Ma (P. P. Song et al., 2020), and ultimately reaching∼ 33.4 ± 3.0°N during 213–204 Ma (P. P. Song
∼et al., 2015) (in Zaduo reference). The trajectory indicates that the EQT drifted slow∼ly northward at a rate of
during 297–259 Ma, then drifted rapidly northward at a velocity of 20.6 ± 8.9 cm/yr during
~52.509 c–m25/1y rMa and ∼13.5 ± 6.5 cm/yr during 251–240 Ma (Figure 3). The latter tw∼o estimated velocities are
s∼imilar to that of th∼e Himalayan Terrane ( 15.4 cm/yr) prior to its collision with the Lhasa Terrane (T. S.
Yang et al., 2015) and the Indian Plate (15–∼20 cm/yr) during the 70–55 Ma time interval (Besse & Courtil-
lot, 2002; Van Hinsbergen et al., 2011; Yi et al., 2011). The accele∼ration of the drift rate after ca. 259 Ma for

the EQT was synchronous to the eruption of the Emeishan large igneous province in the SCB during the
Late Permian ( 260 Ma, Guo et al., 2004). We suspect that the acceleration was likely caused by the eruption
due to the push∼ing away mechanism, as the EQT was located on the west of the SCB, based on the similar
bimodal volcanic rocks (Liu et., 2016; J. Wang et al., 2018), paleolatitudes (Ma et al., 2019), and fauna and
flora fossils (Metcalfe, 2013; G. C. Zhao et al., 2018) between the EQT and the SCB.
Regardless of inclination bias in sedimentary rocks, among the excluded relatively high quality paleo-
magnetic results (only fail Criterion 1 with large age uncertainties), the Late Carboniferous-Early Permi-
an ( 23.5 ± 2.2°S, X. F. Yang et al., 2017) and the Late Triassic ( 30.4 ± 4.0°N, C. Y. Song et al., 2012;
31.∼8 ± 5.6°N, Zhou et al., 2019) ones more or less fall along the∼ northward drift path (Figure 3), like-
∼ly implying that their assigned ages may be reliable. Thus, the three paleomagnetic data sets (C. Y. Song
et al., 2012; X. F. Yang et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2019) are more likely high quality and can be directly used in
future related analyses. In addition, for the paleomagnetic result of K. N. Huang et al. (1992), putting their
paleolatitude of 4.6 ± 6.1°N on our best fit line will yield a rough mean age of 253 Ma, which is younger
than the proposed ages of both K. N. Huang et al. (1992) and TARGS (2007); Further numerical age studies
are necessary.
5.2. Implication for the Closure of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean
It is widely accepted that the paleolatitudinal overlap of the EQT with the Tarim Block indicates the colli-
sion of the two and the closure of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean (Ma et al., 2019; Song et al, 2015, 2017, 2020; Yan
et al., 2016, 2019; Zhou et al., 2019). For the Tarim Block, we adopted B. C. Huang et al. (2018)'s poles and
converted their paleolatitudes into our studied location (32.5°N, 95.2°E; Figure 3 and Table S4). There was
insignificant paleolatitudinal variation throughout the Permo-Triassic for the Tarim Block, with a mean
paleolatitude of 33.0° ± 5.6°N (Figure 3).
∼
Based on the paleo-positions of the Tarim Block and the drift history of the EQT, we now can evaluate the
relative evolution of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean during the Permo-Triassic. (1) The EQT drifted away from the
Gondwana supercontinent from 22.4 ± 4.7°S at 297 Ma (P. P. Song et al., 2017), indicating a wide Jinsha
Ocean (eastern Paleo-Tethys Ocean) of 6,100 ∼± 560 km ( 55.4 ± 5.1° latitudinal differences) between
the Tarim Block and the EQT; (2) The EQ∼T reached a paleola∼titude of 10.0 ± 3.3°N at 251 Ma in Gongjue
area, resulting in a 2,500 ± 470 km ( 23.0 ± 4.3° latitudinal differences) wide Paleo∼-Jinsha Ocean at the
P/T boundary; (3) T∼he EQT drifted to ∼a paleolatitude of 23.5 ± 5.6°N at 240 Ma (P. P. Song et al., 2020),
implying a 1,040 ± 610 km wide Paleo-Jinsha Ocean at this time; (4) th∼e EQT reached a paleolatitude of
33.0° ± 5.∼6°N, and the EQT overlapped with the Tarim Block at 209 Ma (P. P. Song et al., 2015). There-
∼fore, we hypothesize that the collision of the EQT with the Tarim B∼lock must have occurred sometime be-
tween 240 and 209 Ma. However, there are no reliable paleomagnetic results in the EQT for this key time
period ∼that can be used to estimate the closure age of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean (Figure 3).
Extrapolating a constant northward velocity to estimate a continental collision time has been widely used
in tectonic applications of paleomagnetism (e.g., Ma et al., 2014; 2018; 2019; Lippert et al., 2014; T. S. Yang
et al., 2015). Based on the age (251–240 Ma) and latitudinal (10°N–23.5°N) differences, a mean velocity
of 13.5 cm/yr was obtained for the EQT. By extrapolating this velocity, it would take 7.7 ± 4.5 Ma for
the∼ EQT to collide with the Tarim Block at 33.0 ± 5.6°N after 240 Ma. Thus, this veloci∼ty estimate would
provide a lowermost age of 232.3 ± 4.5 M∼a for the closure age of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean in the region
(Figure 3). However, if we a∼ssign a best fit line for the paleolatitudes of the EQT at 297 Ma, 259 Ma,
251 Ma, 240 Ma, and 209 Ma, the collision of the EQT with the Tarim Block wou∼ld have oc∼curred at
∼220 Ma. T∼herefore, we hypothesize that the collision of the EQT with the Tarim Block and the closure of
∼the Paleo-Tethys Ocean have probably occurred between 232 and 220 Ma (Figure 3).
∼ ∼
To better understand the collision process of the EQT with the Tarim Block/NCB, some other lines of evi-
dence are considered (Table S5). For example, a recent integrated paleomagnetic study in Yanshiping, Cen-
tral Qiangtang reveal an apparent change in rotational senses from counterclockwise to clockwise of the
Qiangtang terrane during 230–225 Ma, attributed to the Qiangtang - Songpan-Ganzi collision (M. D. Yan
et al., 2016); Based on a Late Triassic (Carnian Stage) paleomagnetic result from Yunnan, the EQT-Indo-

### page_8
Geophysical Research Letters 10.1029/2020GL092059
china Terranes were located at 26°N, a latitude that overlapped with the Tarim Block/NCB, indicating the
northern branch of the Paleo-T∼ethys Ocean was north of the EQT and closed no later than the early Late
Triassic (235–230 Ma; Y. G. Yan et al., 2019); A provenance analysis of the light and heavy minerals of Late
Triassic sandstone samples from the Western Songpan-Ganzi terrane shows that collision related turbidite
deposits commenced at 230 Ma in this area (K. J. Zhang et al., 2008); Geochronologic and geochemical
analysis of intrusive rock∼s cutting the turbidite deposits in the Songpan-Ganzi terrane indicate that defor-
mation and thickening of the Middle-Late Triassic gravity flow deposits occurred during the Late Triassic
(L. Y. Zhang et al., 2014), suggesting an age of collision of Qiangtang Terrane and Kunlun arc of Late Trias-
sic; Collision related unconformities are widespread between the Middle and Upper Triassic strata, such as
in the southeastern (e.g., Zaduo, Zhiduo, and Markam; QGS, 2005; TARGS, 2007) and northern margins of
the EQT (BGMRXAR, 1993), implying collision between the EQT and the north continents and the closure
of the Paleo-Jinsha Ocean occurred by the early Late Triassic; The Upper Triassic molasse deposits are ex-
posed along the northern margins of the EQT (BGMRXAR, 1993), indicating that the syn-collisional event
occurred in the Late Triassic; The emplacement age of the hosting rock (i.e., adamellite) of 226 Ma in Gong-
jue area, indicating that the eclogites had undergone fast exhumation before 226 Ma, and the continent-con-
tinent collision of the Zhongza and Qamdo terranes was in the Late Triassic (Tang et al., 2020). Moreover,
reliable geologic, paleomagnetic, and paleontologic evidence suggest the closure of the Mianlue Ocean be-
tween the southern (e.g., SCB, Indochina, Sibumasu, WQT-Lhasa, and EQT) and the northern (e.g., NCB
and North Qinling, Alex, Central Qilian, Tarim, and Qaidam terranes) continents and the formation of the
E-W-trending Central China Orogenic System occurred before 220 Ma (G. C. Zhao et al., 2018). In addi-
tion, the Heri granodioritic rocks in the West Qinling area were e∼mplaced in the Late Triassic (235–223 Ma),
indicating the closure of the Paleo-A’nimaque-Mianlue Ocean occurred at 235–223 Ma (Xing et al., 2020).
Overall, based on the lines of evidence above, we hypothesize that the collision of the EQT with the Tarim
Block and the closure of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean probably occurred at 232–220 Ma, most likely at about
230 Ma (Figure S6). ∼
6. Conclusions
Zircon U-Pb dating of three samples of volcanic rocks from the top, middle and bottom of the Gadikao Fm.
provide high quality age control of for this previously assumed Carboniferous or Permian
formation. Rock magnetic, field tests ~a2n5d4 p–2al4e8o sMecaular variation analyses suggest the presence of a primary,
Permo-Triassic boundary magnetization in the samples. Paleomagnetic analysis yield a high quality (29
sites 257 samples) robust paleomagnetic pole of 59.7°N and 228.2°E (A = 3.3°) at 251 Ma, corresponding
95
to a paleolatitude of 10.0 ± 3.3°N (reference point at 32.5°N and 95.2°E). Integrated∼ with other reliable pale-
omagnetic data and other lines of geologic evidence, we hypothesize that the closure of the Paleo-Tethys
Ocean in the Qamdo region were best estimated at 232–220 Ma, most likely at about 230 Ma.
